1:
The chapter is read against the one before it, and the reversal is the point. Matthew Henry sets them side by side: there a fruitful country was turned into a horrid wilderness, here a wilderness into good land; when the land was freed from the Assyrian army the ravaged districts began to recover, and when the Gentile nations, long a wilderness bringing forth no fruit to God, received the gospel, joy came with it. John Wesley makes the solitary place the seat of God's church. John Calvin describes the same change, that having foretold the turning of Edom into a desert the prophet promises fertility to the wilderness, and insists it is God's own work, since he waters some parts of the earth more bountifully than others and afterwards withdraws the blessing for men's ingratitude. Charles Ellicott makes it a contrast between the desolation of the chief enemy and the renewed beauty of Israel's inheritance, and takes the three nouns for three degrees in the absence of culture.

How far the promise reaches is stated most fully by Adam Clarke. The images are so consolatory and sublime, he says, that they oblige us to extend their fulfilment to the period when the Messiah shall take his great power and reign; two verses were literally accomplished by our Saviour and his apostles, but the context makes plain those miracles were not the whole import, so the words have a further application, following on God's judgments against the enemies of the Church. Calvin comes at it from the other end, passing by what he calls the dreams of the Jewish expositors, who apply every such passage to a temporal reign of the Messiah.

The flower has its own small dispute. Ellicott would render it the narcissus, though primrose and crocus have both been proposed. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same three: one ancient paraphrase gives the narcissus while the paraphrase here leaves the word indefinite as lilies, and the name itself points to a bulbous plant, probably the crocus and primrose, which were classed together and may easily be confounded, whereas narcissus and primrose have nothing in common except that both grow from bulbs.

The doubled verb draws a characteristic reading from Calvin: it may denote either unbroken vegetation, so that the land shall not flower with a fading blossom and sink back into its old foulness but bloom continually, or else the daily increase of improvement, since Christ adds to his grace in us from day to day. Ellicott sets the three names of cultivated beauty against the three of desolation, and observes that over this land will shine not the common light of day but the glory of the Lord.

Clarke works the text hard: for one word the Greek read another and rendered it the deserts of Jordan, and two scholars proposed the banks of Jordan.

Who is told to strengthen the weak hands is settled by the verse that follows. Calvin allows that the words might be taken generally, of everyone whose hands are feeble and whose knees totter, but says the next verse shows the passage to concern the ministers of the word, who are to arouse and encourage men whose hearts are broken; the charge is seasonable, since so many tokens of God's anger could not but fill even the strongest minds with alarm. John Wesley agrees in a line, addressing the ministers of God; John Gill assigns the words to the prophet. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion differently: since the New Testament quotes the clause figuratively, the words here are figurative too. Gill glosses the fearful heart as the hasty heart, belonging to men ready to fly from the enemy and inconsiderate of the promises. Ellicott connects the encouragement with the words a king of Judah used in the same crisis, king and prophet alike grounding their comfort in the righteousness of God's government.
5:
Whether the cures are of the body or of the soul is the question the passage forces, and most take both. John Gill says the words were literally fulfilled at the first coming of Christ and spiritually among Jews and Gentiles alike, especially under the apostles' ministry, when men blind in spiritual things had their understanding opened to see their own sinfulness and the suitableness of a Saviour. Matthew Henry keeps the miracles bodily and lists them from the Gospels, sight given with a word to one born blind, the ears of the deaf unstopped by a single command, the lame given the use of their limbs; he sets them under wonders wrought in nature and grace together, sufficient to prove that it is no less than God who comes. John Wesley reads it all of the poor Gentiles, once blind and deaf, whose minds now have eyes and ears opened.

John Calvin approaches it as a reversal of an earlier sentence. The prophet probably alludes, he says, to his own former threatening of dreadful blindness and stupefaction of soul against the Jews, and since a true restoration is accomplished by Christ we must come to him if we wish to know what these words mean. Keil and Delitzsch state the frame: amid such miracles the people of God are redeemed and led home to Zion.

Calvin turns the waters that follow into a doctrine of provision: there is no reason to dread want once we are reconciled to God through Christ, and though wicked men often have great abundance, their wealth is wretched, since they have not Christ, from whom alone a salutary abundance proceeds.

The word for the parched ground is where the tile's real interest lies, and three of them independently identify it. Adam Clarke observes that the word is Arabic as well as Hebrew and means the same in both, the glowing sandy plain that at a distance looks like water; he quotes the Koran, where the works of unbelievers are like a vapour on a plain that the thirsty traveller takes for water until he comes and finds nothing, and a commentator's note that it means the false appearance seen on sandy plains about noon, a large lake in motion caused by the sun's beams on the quivering vapours.

Charles Ellicott identifies it as what we now call the mirage, the sheen that looks like a sparkling lake and proves to be barren sand, and takes the promise to be that in place of the delusive show there shall be the lake itself. He corrects two words in the next clause: the creatures whose lair the desert was are better called jackals than dragons, and the grass is better read as growing to the height of reeds and rushes.

Calvin reaches the same identification and marks it as a gain on the older commentators. Those who followed the Greek and Latin, he reports, gave the word only a general sense of dryness, but it is now agreed that it denotes the illusive appearance caused by unequal refraction in the lower air; in the deserts of Arabia and Africa it presents precisely an extensive sheet of water, which not only misleads the traveller but aggravates his thirst by the disappointment.

Gill and Wesley take the verse spiritually. Gill applies it to men scorched with a sense of divine wrath and thirsting after grace, and to those scorched by persecution. Wesley makes the dry places fruitful, meaning the effusion of God's grace on nations wholly destitute of it, and notes that the reeds and rushes named grow only in moist ground. Gill reads the leaping of the lame the same way, of men impotent to any good, with neither will nor power to go to Christ, who by the Spirit became able and willing and ran in his ways.
8:
That the highway and the way are one road, not two, is agreed. John Gill says these are not two ways but one, a way cast up above the ground; John Wesley says the same, a causeway that is raised earth and a road at once. Adam Clarke holds that the second word was added to the first clause by mistake, sixteen manuscripts and three versions having it only once.

Where the road leads divides them. Charles Ellicott takes it for a raised causeway, and rejects the reading that refers it to the return of the exiles: it is rather the road by which the pilgrims of all nations shall journey to the mountain of the Lord's house, its name confirming that, a true sacred way to the earthly temple as a type of the eternal one not made with hands. John Calvin begins with the return, promised so the exiles might not think themselves banished for ever, but extends it much farther, to places once uninhabited now filled with the journeys of a vast multitude and a land so at peace that men may pass without fear, since where there are no inhabitants there can be no roads. Gill makes the road Christ himself, the only way of salvation, cast up above the mire of sin.

Clarke disputes a clause the others pass over. Where our version says the way shall be for those, he would read that God himself shall be with them, walking in the way, the older English version having translated it so while the later translators were misled by the Jewish division of the sentence. Wesley keeps the received sense, the road being for the weak and lame whom God will lead, and so plain that even the most foolish travellers cannot mistake it.

Ellicott recalls that lions had not ceased to haunt the Jordan valley as in the days of the judges and early kings, and that the recent emptying of the northern kingdom had laid the country more open to them; he would render the second phrase not any ravenous beast but the most ravenous. Gill takes the lions for wicked men, savage toward God's people, who once brought into this way become as tame as lambs. Calvin sets the verse against the curse of an earlier chapter, where wild beasts were to meet the Jews wherever they went, and draws the doctrine that God not only begins but carries through our salvation.

The words for the redeemed and the ransomed produce a flat contradiction. Clarke builds his reading on the idea of price: the first word means those whose forfeited inheritances are recovered by the kinsman, which he says all orthodox divines have referred to the incarnation and sacrifice of our Lord, and the second comes from a root meaning to redeem by paying a price. Ellicott denies exactly that: the Hebrew words express simply the idea of release and freedom, without implying, as the English words do, a payment as its condition. Gill keeps to the effect, the ransomed being turned from darkness to light and returned from straying to the Shepherd of souls.

The close draws two very different final comments. Ellicott says the first volume ends fitly with a picture that carries thought beyond any earthly fulfilment, and suggests its imagery began from the processions of pilgrims who came up to the temple singing at their halting-places; these are the closing words of the prophet's political activity, written probably in his old age. Clarke ends on the sound of a single word, saying no sorrowful accent was ever better expressed than the strong guttural term used here for sighing, nearly the same as the cry of Irish funeral wailing, a whole nation putting its mournful accents into three syllables. Keil and Delitzsch print the last two verses together as the chapter's single closing movement.
